t: Decode XORed Array — Rebuilding Hidden Values One XOR at a Time
o:
We have a hidden array `arr` of `n` non-negative integers and its length-(n−1) companion `encoded`, where `encoded[i] = arr[i] XOR arr[i+1]`. Along with `encoded` we are handed `arr[0]` (called `first`) and asked to recover the whole original array.

Take Example 1: `encoded = [1,2,3]`, `first = 1`. We know `arr[0] = 1`; rewriting the relation gives `arr[i+1] = encoded[i] XOR arr[i]`, so `arr[1] = 1 XOR 1 = 0`, then `arr[2] = 2 XOR 0 = 2`, and finally `arr[3] = 3 XOR 2 = 1`, producing `[1,0,2,1]` exactly as expected. Example 2 works identically: starting from 4 and peeling off `6, 2, 7, 3` yields `[4,2,0,7,4]`.

The entire problem hinges on one algebraic fact: XOR is its own inverse, so `a XOR b = c` implies `b = a XOR c`. Because every element is chained to its predecessor, knowing just `arr[0]` unlocks everything in a single left-to-right pass. The constraints (`n ≤ 10^4`) make any linear scan trivially fast — no search, no data structures.
k: XOR is self-inverse: from encoded[i] = arr[i] XOR arr[i+1] we get arr[i+1] = encoded[i] XOR arr[i].
One known element (first) anchors the whole chain — each recovered value reveals the next.
The answer is unique and derivable greedily, so a single forward pass with no search suffices.

a.i: Start the output with `first`. Every subsequent value follows directly from the previous one and the corresponding encoded entry, because XOR-ing both sides of `encoded[i] = arr[i] ^ arr[i+1]` with `arr[i]` isolates `arr[i+1]`. No auxiliary structure is needed beyond the result array itself.
s: Initialize the result array with first.
For each value e in encoded, append (previous value XOR e) to the result.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over encoded, constant work per element.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary beyond the O(n) output array.

w: Present this greedy forward pass immediately — it is the intended solution. Pitfalls: off-by-one slips between encoded indices and output indices, and forgetting that `first` is given (its absence is exactly what makes LC 1734 harder). Edge cases: minimum length n = 2. Follow-ups: what if `first` were unknown (see Decode XORed Permutation, where the odd-length permutation property pins it down), or how the decoding changes if the mixing operation were addition instead of XOR?
